model_names_check.detail: Source: 'agents powered by Anthropic's upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet (released October 2024)'. Row says 'Claude 3.5 Sonnet' — correct but omits 'upgraded' (Oct 2024 version); the distinction matters because the blog explicitly contrasts it with 'the prior version of Claude 3.5 Sonnet'. Source also notes AgentDojo found it 'one of the top performing models in resisting agent hijacking attacks' — i.e., the 81% was achieved against one of the most robust models.

overstatement_check: OVERSTATEMENT: the Finding's final sentence 'Current agentic AI defences are critically insufficient against determined adversaries' is an editorial conclusion that appears nowhere in the source. The blog's actual framing is measured — 'Some defenses against hijacking attacks are available and continuing to evaluate the efficacy of these defenses against new attacks is another important area for future work'. The blog draws methodological lessons about evaluations, not a verdict that defences are 'critically insufficient'. Additionally, 'baseline defences' inverts the source's 'strongest baseline attack' (see numbers_check), inflating the apparent attack-vs-defence gap.
notes: Three issues beyond the above. (1) Report Title 'CAISI AI Agent Hijacking Evaluations -- 81% attack success rate' is not the source title; actual title: 'Technical Blog: Strengthening AI Agent Hijacking Evaluations'. Embedding a finding in the title field is editorializing. (2) Institution: current page is 'Authored by Technical Staff at the Center for AI Standards and Innovation' and credits red teaming 'in collaboration with red teamers at the UK AI Security Institute', supporting the JOINT coding — but note the page was 'Released January 17, 2025, Updated December 19, 2025'; at original publication the US body was the US AI Safety Institute (renamed CAISI in June 2025) and the UK body was the AI Safety Institute (renamed Feb 2025), so 'US CAISI' is anachronistic for a 2025-01-17 publication though it matches the page as it stands today. (3) The 81% figure is specific to the Workspace environment (held-out user tasks); attacks 'were also successful' when transferred to the other three environments but the 81% number itself is Workspace-only — the Finding's unqualified phrasing slightly overgeneralizes.
